steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on adversarial attacks against speaker identification, covering attack detection, attack classification and identifying the victim model. Give the background on adversarial attacks and countermeasures, say how we extend earlier attack-classification work, list our contributions, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Neural networks for speech and their vulnerability to adversarial attacks
2. Countermeasures and prior attack classification work
3. What this paper does
4. Contributions
5. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- neural nets: strong performance on speech tasks, e.g. automatic speech recognition, speaker recognition
- susceptible to adversarial attacks -> concerns about robustness, reliability
- small (usually) imperceptible input perturbations -> misclassification; speech: (almost) imperceptible noise drastically changes outputs
- white-box (model parameters available to adversary) vs black-box (not available)
- white-box usually more powerful, faster to generate; black-box queries model many times
- pre-trained models widely available -> white-box feasible, bigger threat

2. Countermeasures
- focus: speaker recognition
- range of countermeasures emerged
- two categories: proactive defenses (more robust models), reactive countermeasures (filter out attacks)
- prior work: countermeasure that classifies between attacks, applied to speaker identification and verification

3. This paper
- extend prior work, improve multiple parts of classification system
- leverage insights from attack mechanisms -> comprehensive defense framework
- experiments: detect presence of attack, classify attack type
- new: identify victim model; new dataset of attacks on a range of speaker identification networks
- bridge attack detection and attack classification -> more resilient, trustworthy ML systems

4. Contributions
- binary attack detection + ablation omitting attack types in training
- new architectures for attack classification
- new dataset, attacks on four victim models
- classify amongst victim models using it

5. Organization
- Sec 2 previous classification system, chosen attacks; Sec 3 dataset; Sec 4 threat models (attacks, norms, victim models, dataset building); Sec 5 experiments; Sec 6 results; Sec 7 discussion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Neural networks have changed a lot of domains, and they show remarkable performance on a range of speech tasks, like automatic speech recognition or speaker recognition. But these networks are susceptible to adversarial attacks, and this has raised significant concerns about how robust and reliable they are. Adversarial attacks exploit vulnerabilities in neural networks and cause misclassification or erroneous behavior through perturbations to the input data that are (usually) small and imperceptible. For speech, this means an (almost) imperceptible noise that can drastically change the outputs of a system. These attacks can be white-box attacks, when the adversary has the network model parameters, or black-box attacks, when the adversary does not have the network model parameters. White-box attacks are usually more powerful and take comparatively shorter time to generate than black-box attacks, which have to query the model multiple times to generate an attack. Since pre-trained models are widely available, white-box attacks are feasible, which increases the threat they represent. In this work we focus on speaker recognition systems. Because of the threat to these systems, a range of countermeasures have emerged. These countermeasures fall into two broad categories: proactive defenses that make the models more robust, and reactive countermeasures that filter out adversarial attacks. Prior work introduced a new countermeasure strategy that classifies between different attacks, applied on speaker identification and verification systems.

This paper
- extend prior attack-classification work, improve multiple parts of the classification system
- insights from attack mechanisms -> comprehensive defense framework
- experiments: detect presence of attack, classify attack type
- identify victim model; new dataset of attacks on a range of speaker identification networks
- bridge detection and classification -> more resilient, trustworthy ML systems

Contributions
- binary attack detection + ablation omitting attack types in training
- new architectures for attack classification
- new dataset, attacks targeting four victim models
- classify amongst victim models

Organization
- Sec 2 previous classification system + attacks; Sec 3 dataset; Sec 4 threat models (attacks, norms, victim models, building datasets); Sec 5 experiments; Sec 6 results; Sec 7 discussion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Neural networks have changed a lot of domains, and they show remarkable performance on a range of speech tasks, like automatic speech recognition or speaker recognition. But these networks are susceptible to adversarial attacks, and this has raised significant concerns about how robust and reliable they are. Adversarial attacks exploit vulnerabilities in neural networks and cause misclassification or erroneous behavior through perturbations to the input data that are (usually) small and imperceptible. For speech, this means an (almost) imperceptible noise that can drastically change the outputs of a system. These attacks can be white-box attacks, when the adversary has the network model parameters, or black-box attacks, when the adversary does not have the network model parameters. White-box attacks are usually more powerful and take comparatively shorter time to generate than black-box attacks, which have to query the model multiple times to generate an attack. Since pre-trained models are widely available, white-box attacks are feasible, which increases the threat they represent. In this work we focus on speaker recognition systems. Because of the threat to these systems, a range of countermeasures have emerged. These countermeasures fall into two broad categories: proactive defenses that make the models more robust, and reactive countermeasures that filter out adversarial attacks. Prior work introduced a new countermeasure strategy that classifies between different attacks, applied on speaker identification and verification systems.

In this paper we extend that work and improve multiple parts of the classification system. Our approach uses insights from adversarial attack mechanisms to develop a comprehensive defense framework. With extensive experiments and analysis we show that our method works well for accurately detecting whether there is an attack and for classifying the type of adversarial attack. We also propose a method to identify the victim model that the attack was performed on. To do this, we generate a new dataset of attacks computed on a range of speaker identification networks. By bridging the gap between attack detection and attack classification, our work is a significant step towards building machine learning systems that are more resilient and trustworthy against evolving adversarial threats.

Our main contributions are:

- A binary adversarial attack detection system, plus an ablation study on what happens when different types of adversarial attacks are left out during training.

- New architectures for the attack classification system.

- A new dataset with different adversarial attacks targeting four different victim models.

- Using this dataset to classify amongst victim models.

Section 2 presents the previous classification system that this work is based on in detail, and also the adversarial attacks we focus on. Section 3 presents the dataset used for all our experiments. Section 4 presents the threat models we study: what attacks, norms and victim models are considered, and how the datasets containing all those threat models are built. Section 5 presents our classification and detection experiments, Section 6 shows the results, and Section 7 discusses them.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Neural networks have revolutionized various domains, showing remarkable performance on a range of speech-related tasks, such as automatic speech recognition [1] or speaker recognition [2]. However, the susceptibility of these networks to adversarial attacks [3,4,5] has raised significant concerns about their robustness and reliability [6,7]. Adversarial attacks exploit vulnerabilities in neural networks, causing misclassification or erroneous behavior through (usually) small, imperceptible perturbations to the input data. Applied to speech, this takes the form of an (almost) imperceptible noise that can drastically change the outputs of a given system. These attacks can be either white-box attacks (when the network model parameters are available to the adversary) or black-box attacks (when they are not). White-box attacks are usually more powerful and take comparatively less time to generate than black-box attacks, which rely on querying the model multiple times. With the widespread availability of pre-trained models, white-box attacks are feasible, which increases the threat they represent. In this work, we focus on speaker recognition systems. In response to the threat to these systems, a range of countermeasures [8,9,10] have emerged. These countermeasures can be classified into two broad categories: proactive defenses that make the models more robust, and reactive countermeasures that filter out adversarial attacks. [11,12] introduced a novel countermeasure strategy designed to classify between different attacks, applied to speaker identification and verification systems.

In this paper, we extend this work by improving multiple parts of the classification system. Our approach leverages insights from adversarial attack mechanisms to develop a comprehensive defense framework. Through extensive experimentation and analysis, we demonstrate that our method is effective at accurately detecting the presence of an attack and classifying the type of adversarial attack. Additionally, we propose a method to identify the victim model on which the attack was performed. To this end, we generate a new dataset of attacks computed on a range of speaker identification networks. By bridging the gap between attack detection and attack classification, our work is a significant step towards building more resilient and trustworthy machine learning systems in the face of evolving adversarial threats.

Our main contributions can be summarized as:

- Development of a binary adversarial attack detection system, together with an ablation study exploring the impact of omitting different types of adversarial attacks during training.

- Exploration of new architectures for the attack classification system.

- Introduction of a new dataset featuring different adversarial attacks targeting four different victim models.

- Use of this dataset to classify amongst victim models.

Section 2 presents in detail the previous classification system this work is based on, as well as the adversarial attacks we focus on. Section 3 then presents the dataset used for all our experiments, followed by Section 4, which presents the threat models studied here: which attacks, norms and victim models are considered, and how the datasets containing all those threat models are built. Section 5 presents our classification and detection experiments, whose results are shown in Section 6 and discussed in Section 7.
